title: Declaration of Interdependence
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart reads two poems, one that calls on us to release the myth of independence and one that imagines a woman sharing a last dinner with Death. Between them, Kanho describes a week of sesshin with the Everyday Zen community, led by Norman Fischer, where meditation kept circling interbeing and the blackened teeth on a bronze Manjushri's lion kept turning into an obsession with flossing. Plums from a neighbor, shipped from Chile, can't be returned to any tree, and a pig never needed lipstick. Both images lead to gratitude and to a body replaced every seven years. Kanho ends by saying the second poem means a new book of poems to buy.

sentences.text: So, my dharma talk is going to be a little bit on the strange side tonight, and thank you ahead of time for putting up with that.
I was in sesshin this last week with the Everyday Zen community.
So that underlay what came up, and also the passing away of our good dharma friend, Edie Norton.
And Norman's dharma talks, everything got mixed up, and then I found this beautiful poem.
So here's the first of two poems I'm going to read tonight.
*May we release the myth of independence and make a declaration to embrace and nourish our interdependence.
May we pledge allegiance to the land, to the waters, to our human and non-human kin, to the earth body we call home.
May we find our house of worship in the trees, the sky, the dirt, the mountains, in our own bodies.
May we find new places of power shimmering along the edges of what we think is the only way forward.
May we love each other and honor life more than we love guns, oil, money, power, control, or the written word of hungry ghosts.
May we midwife systems of harm to divest grace and compose them into new ways of caring for each other.
May we honor our grief, make space for depressed, find pleasure in our pursuit for justice, and ignite transformation with our holy rage.*
Gina Porrell is the person who wrote this poem.
So, how are you tonight?
I'm really happy to see you.
Last week I was in California sitting sesshin with the Everyday Zen community, and it was led by my teacher Norman Fischer.
It was really wonderful, at Santa Sabina.
No need to say or do.
Just roll out of bed when you hear the wake-up bell and just be.
Finding freedom while sitting, and thoughts, some deep, some silly, rise and fall away.
I'll tell you a silly one right now.
I was facing the wall, but in front of the wall was a cabinet, and on that cabinet was a statue of Manjushri and his lion.
It was made of bronze, and they had blackened parts of the statue to create more contrast.
It was really nice.
But one of the things that was blackened was the tiger's, the lion's teeth.
After about day two or three, I started obsessing about brushing and flossing those lion teeth.
That they shouldn't be black, it's just wrong.
Every time the thought came up, I did the gentle Zen thing: thank you for sharing, please now go away.
But it didn't work very well, the going away part.
On the more serious side, many of my meditations circled around interdependence, and as Thich Nhat Hanh used to call it, interbeing.
Holding the thought of interbeing, the circle continuously changed, or widened, or got smaller in some spots.
Breathing with and for all beings.
Slowly counting my exhales from one to ten until there was some stability, or sometimes I just didn't get past three.
Living for and with all beings, in the room and in the world.
What is world?
What is I?
Connections.
Connections.
Dependent co-arising.
Walking into a Zen hall and falling into Indra's net.
Nothing to hold on to and everything changing.
We are supported by the everything.
Instead of being held by the solid, we are carried through birth and life and death by impermanence.
When I let go of fear, the experience can inform me just as it is, not just as I imagine it to be.
When I let go of fixed ideas, I am free to experience everything anew.
"Oh, she doesn't like me.
What did I do wrong?" can turn into "Hello, old friend.
How have you been?"
Because in the end, there's only love and there's only consciousness that binds our universe together.
Likes and dislikes become stronger in isolation.
When one feels alone, when one feels lonely, when one does not feel like a member of the tribe, it is hard to keep dislike from growing.

When I lie on the grass with the sun in my face, with outstretched arms, I meditate that I am the sky, the sun, the rain, shining on all equally, love and blessing alike, living life fully, loving as hard as I can, saying yes, this too.
To love, to pain, to sorrow, to saying hello and to saying goodbye.
Have you ever tried to return something to its origin?
It can't be done.
The plums I just ate were a gift from my neighbors.
Maybe thank you for the fresh bread I brought over yesterday.
Well, the plums, I mean, not the neighbors.
They came in from Chile.
The tree also won't take them back, even if I found the right tree.
The tree won't take them back because the plums' time as part of the tree has passed, or it is yet to come.
That little plum can become a big tree, but even if I could do that, how can I return sun and rain back to their source?
Also, the pig did not need any lipstick to begin with.
It was perfectly fine in its piggishness.
It's only when the outsider looks in that they may think the lipstick is necessary, because they want the pig to be something different.
The pig is happy doing pig things, and its snout is perfectly fine.
It can find truffles better than any dog.
It does not need the lipstick to disguise its failings, because what others may perceive as failings is just that the pig has never been anything but a pig.
The pig also has never tried to be something different.
Piggishness is not a failing, it is what it was meant to be.
I don't need any lipstick either.
Well, that's unless my lips are chapped, then I make an exception.
I am my age and getting older, and neither lipstick nor makeup will change that fact.
And it is with deep gratitude that I spend this life.
I am grateful to my sangha in the traditional sense, the fellowship of Buddhist practitioners.
I am grateful that my parents did their best.
I am grateful to my sangha in the wider sense, to all living beings, the trees and the rocks.
I'm grateful to all my teachers, past, present and future.
I am grateful that there is food and a safe place to sleep.
I am grateful for warmth and clean water.
I am grateful.
How will I return all the aggregates to their source?
Every seven years, all my body has been replaced little bit by little bit.
And yet all this time, I thought there was an I, a self.
I believed that there were big changes over the years, a broken this or that, slow changes, a different me compared to yesterday, not so much.

Each perceptibly small moment dying to itself, no way, until we let ourselves become bigger than it can possibly be, so it can include the flower falling from the tree on another continent and a new shoot growing into the sun right in front of my feet.
Maybe, maybe each one of us is a nerve ending through which the universe, God, Buddha nature, consciousness, big self experiences itself?
The same story observed through billions of eyes and other light-perceiving organs.
The same is true for nose, tongue, ear, touch, and all the many ways that humans cannot even imagine.
And like all good stories, one day it ends.
One day I will end.
Causes and conditions, interdependence and interbeing have nourished me so far and continue to support my life to this moment, at least.
And I am a hundred percent certain that at one point in the future, that will change.
This too is just as it is and as it must be.
Here is the second poem.
*Les asked me to join him for dinner.
So I slipped into my favorite black dress that I had been saving for a special occasion and let him walk me to our [unclear: "candlelit chest"].
He ordered ribeye extra rare.
I ordered two desserts and red wine, and then I sipped and wondered why he looked so familiar and smelled like earth and memory.
It felt like a place both far away and deep within my body, a place that whispers to me on the crisp autumn breeze, along the liminal edges of dusk and dawn, somewhere between dancing and stillness.
He looked at me with the endless night sky in his eyes and asked, "Did you live your life, my love?"

As I swirled my wine in the glass, I wondered if I understood the thread I wove into the greater fabric, if I loved in a way that was deep and freeing, if I let pain and grief carve me into something more grateful, if I made enough space to be in awe that flowers exist and take the time to watch the honeybees drink their sweet nectar.

I wondered what the riddles of regret and longing had taught me and if I realized just how beautiful and insignificant and monstrous and small we are for the brief moment that we're here before we all melt back down into ancestors of the land.
Death watched me lick buttercream off my fingers as he leaned in close and said, "My darling, it's time."
So I slipped my hand into his as he slowly walked me home.

I took a deep breath and he leaned in close for the long kiss good night, and I felt a soft laugh leave my lips as his mouth met mine, because I could never resist the man with the lust for my soul in his eyes and the kiss that makes my heart stop.*
So again, I want to thank Sheena Poro for the gift of this poem, because a true gift it was.
If what I said tonight does not resonate with you, please forget every single word, just go on with your [unclear: "size"], and if there was something in there, you're welcome to it.
And now I have to buy another book, poems by Sheena Poro.
I just discovered her today and I was touched.
